projects.title: Axelrod's Razor
projects.problem: Understanding the dynamics of evolutionary game theory, agent cooperation (e.g., Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma), and how strategic choices propagate or decline within complex social networks and decision environments.
projects.context: An interactive web-based simulation sandbox built as a philosophical and mathematical laboratory to study collective intelligence and strategic coordination.
projects.solution: An agent-based modeling simulator that runs high-performance tournament scenarios in-browser. Users can configure game-theory matrices, mutate strategies, and watch spatial distributions evolve over time.
projects.architecture: Rust simulation engine compiled to WebAssembly for native-speed agent updates, wrapped in a Next.js/React frontend with Tailwind CSS and Recharts for live plotting of strategic population dynamics.
projects.decisions: Chose to compile a Rust core to WebAssembly instead of running pure JavaScript to handle 10,000+ spatial agent interactions in real-time at 60 FPS without UI freezing.
projects.tradeoffs: Using WebAssembly increased initial load bundle size and complexity of compilation, but provided a 40x speedup in simulation frame rates, enabling large-scale spatial grid runs.
outcomes: Created a visual sandboxed environment for testing classical game theory strategies (Tit-for-Tat, Grim Trigger, Win-Stay Lose-Shift).
Enabled real-time simulation runs of spatial tournaments on 100x100 grids directly in the browser.
impact: Serves as a flagship exploration of collective decision design, demonstrating the conditions under which cooperation emerges in adversarial networks.
Integrated directly into Mentat Commons' decision workshops as a visual aid to explain gridlocks and alignment failure patterns.
reusable_stories: Scaling spatial grid simulations from 100 to 10,000 agents in-browser using WebAssembly.
Using game theory simulations to model organizational silos and cross-functional conflict.
interview_questions_supported: How do you design high-performance applications that run computationally heavy code in the browser?
Tell me about a project where you applied mathematical or game-theory concepts to solve a practical system design problem.

projects.title: Smart Waste Detection System
projects.problem: Inefficient municipal waste collection and frequent illegal dumping in public areas due to lack of real-time detection and reporting.
projects.context: Deployed under the Bene Data Collective in collaboration with municipal waste management and local community advocates.
projects.solution: Developed an edge-computing pipeline utilizing Raspberry Pi and GPU-accelerated micro-computers running optimized computer vision models (MobileNet SSD) for real-time license plate recognition and waste classification.
projects.architecture: Edge-node computer vision pipelines deploying lightweight PyTorch models in Docker containers on Raspberry Pi 4 units, reporting via MQTT/REST to a centralized Postgres/FastAPI database.
projects.decisions: Opted for edge-based classification and local license plate extraction over cloud processing to avoid high cellular API data fees and to ensure continuous operations in areas with spotty internet connectivity.
projects.tradeoffs: Edge processing limited model depth, requiring extensive pruning and quantization of the object detection network, which slightly reduced detection accuracy under extreme low-light conditions.
outcomes: Successfully deployed across 15 high-risk urban locations with 92% detection uptime.
impact: Reduced response times for illegal dumping cleanup from 48 hours to less than 4 hours.
Saved 20% in municipal route fuel costs through dynamic bin-fullness routing.
reusable_stories: Balancing bandwidth constraints against model performance at the edge.
Navigating privacy concerns with municipal officials and citizens during license plate camera deployment.
interview_questions_supported: Tell me about a time you had to optimize model performance for resource-constrained hardware.
How do you handle privacy and ethical constraints when designing monitoring systems?

projects.title: Solar Panel Optimization Engine
projects.problem: Policy recommenders lacked analytical rigor, leading to sub-optimal solar installation recommendations that failed to align with localized grid capacities.
projects.context: Built for a policy advocacy group seeking to optimize regional energy distribution models.
projects.solution: Developed a mathematical optimization engine integrated into a policy recommender system, combining geospatial solar irradiance data with grid constraints.
projects.architecture: Geospatial vector processing pipelines built with GeoPandas and PostGIS, combined with Python-based linear programming engines running SciPy and PuLP optimization solvers.
projects.decisions: Used linear programming (PuLP/SciPy) for the optimization engine to guarantee global mathematical optimality and high interpretability, rather than employing deep reinforcement learning.
projects.tradeoffs: Linear programming simplified complex non-linear grid behaviors but provided the transparency and speed required by policy makers who needed to audit recommendations.
outcomes: Allowed policy makers to simulate 'what-if' scenarios in real time during legislative workshops.
impact: Increased projected grid integration capacity for solar energy by 35% in simulated regional rollouts.
reusable_stories: Choosing mathematical interpretability over ML hype when advising policy advocates.
Translating geospatial and grid engineering metrics into accessible policy stories.
interview_questions_supported: Describe a situation where you had to explain a complex mathematical model to non-technical stakeholders.

essays.title: Data Without Story, Story Without Data: The False Dichotomy of Decision Systems
essays.summary: An in-depth analysis of why dashboard-driven organizations stall and how structured narratives integrate data to produce better strategic alignment.
essays.content: In modern organizations, data and stories are treated as opposites. This essay argues that decisions require both: data to constrain narratives, and narratives to define what data matters.

research_notes.title: Leakcraft and Mentat Commons: Protecting the Thinking Space
research_notes.summary: Explorations on organizational boundary design and protecting fragile, early-stage ideas from premature metric evaluation.
research_notes.content: Ideas in their infancy need containment. Premature optimization or evaluation destroys novel framings. We need protocols to isolate thinking groups until concepts mature.
